key_terms.meaning: Gate voltage below flat-band pushes majority carriers towards the surface, so the surface holds more of the same carrier type as the bulk.
A gate voltage of the right sign pushes majority carriers away, leaving only fixed ionised dopant atoms under the oxide.
A strong enough gate voltage attracts minority carriers to the surface and forms a thin conducting layer of opposite doping type.
VGS < VTH, so no inversion layer exists and only leakage current flows from drain to source.
VGS > VTH and VDS < VGS − VTH: the channel is continuous and the transistor behaves as a gate-controlled resistor.
The drain-end point where VDS equals the overdrive and the inversion charge density falls to zero.
VDS > VGS − VTH: the channel is pinched off near the drain and the current is set mainly by the overdrive voltage.
VTH: the gate voltage at which surface inversion begins, made up of flat-band voltage, band bending and depletion charge terms.
Rise of VTH when the source is above the body: VTH = VTH0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)), with γ the body-effect coefficient and φF the Fermi potential.
Vov = VGS − VTH: the part of the gate voltage left over to create inversion charge after threshold is met.
Saturation: ID = ½ μnCox(W/L)Vov²; linear: ID = μnCox(W/L)(Vov − VDS/2)VDS, with μn the electron mobility and Cox the oxide capacitance per unit area.
The vertical gate field scatters carriers so the effective mobility falls as the overdrive rises, roughly μeff = μ0/(1 + θVov).
Above a critical lateral field the drift velocity stops rising with field and levels near vsat ≈ 10⁷ cm/s, making ID almost linear in Vov.
The pinch-off point moves towards the source as VDS rises, shortening the effective channel by ΔL and adding the factor (1 + λVDS) to ID.
The oxide capacitance Cox·W·L plus overlap and fringing pieces; the charge the driving stage must supply every cycle.
Cgs and Cgd formed where the gate overlaps the source and drain diffusions; it causes clock feedthrough and adds Miller-multiplied load.
Divide L, W, tox and VDD all by the same factor S so the internal electric fields and the shape of the field pattern stay unchanged.
DIBL: the drain field reaches the source end of a short channel, lowers the source barrier and makes VTH fall as VDS rises.
S ≈ (kT/q)·ln10·(1 + Cd/Cox) mV per decade: how fast ID falls when VGS goes below VTH.
A transistor whose channel is a thin vertical silicon fin with the gate wrapped over two or three sides, giving the gate better control of a short channel.

takeaways: A MOS capacitor becomes a transistor once the gate voltage inverts the surface and the source and drain contact that inversion layer.
Accumulation, depletion and inversion are three states of surface charge; cutoff, linear and saturation are three shapes of the inversion channel.
Threshold voltage is a voltage budget: flat-band, band bending and depletion charge are paid first, and only what remains becomes inversion charge.
The square-law equations are a long-channel, low-field model: current depends on overdrive voltage, W/L and Cox, and turns quadratic in saturation.
Velocity saturation, mobility degradation and channel length modulation are the three corrections that turn the square law into a usable real-device model.
Every terminal pair of a MOSFET is a capacitor; the driver charges and discharges these capacitances, and series resistances slow the charging.
Below threshold the device still conducts exponentially, and that leakage plus gate and junction leakage is now a large share of chip power.
When scaling made planar gates lose control of the channel, the FinFET recovered control by wrapping the gate around a thin fin.
bank_note: Long answers here are expected to move from the MOS capacitor picture to the region-by-region I-V equations, then to non-ideal effects, capacitances and short-channel/FinFET corrections, with clean sketches and labelled symbols.

bank.q: Describe the MOS capacitor in accumulation, depletion and inversion. Draw the charge distribution and the small-signal capacitance-voltage curve, and say what each region means for a transistor.
outline: Sketch of gate, oxide, semiconductor with terminal labels
Accumulation: majority carriers at surface, capacitance ≈ Cox
Depletion: ionised dopants, capacitance in series with depletion capacitance, minimum capacitance point
Inversion: minority-carrier layer, capacitance returns to Cox at low frequency
Strong inversion defined as surface potential reaching 2φF

bank.q: Define threshold voltage of an nMOS transistor and derive its expression from the flat-band voltage, surface potential and depletion charge.
outline: Flat-band voltage and work-function difference
Surface potential 2φF at strong inversion
Depletion charge QB = √(2qεsiNA(2φF))
VTH = VFB + 2φF + QB/Cox
Meaning of each symbol and typical values for a modern process

bank.q: Write the drain current equations of an nMOS transistor in cutoff, linear and saturation, and state the condition that selects each region.
outline: Region conditions in terms of VGS, VTH and VDS
Linear: ID = μnCox(W/L)(Vov − VDS/2)VDS
Saturation: ID = ½μnCox(W/L)Vov²
Continuity of the two branches at VDS = Vov
Definition of each symbol with units

bank.q: List the capacitances of a MOSFET and explain where each one physically comes from.
outline: Oxide capacitance Cox·W·L split into gate-source and gate-drain parts by region of operation
Overlap capacitances Cgs and Cgd from gate over diffusions
Junction capacitances of source-body and drain-body
Fringing and gate-to-contact coupling
Which capacitances dominate in cutoff, linear and saturation

bank.q: An nMOS has μnCox = 200 µA/V², W/L = 10, VTH = 0.5 V and VGS = 1.5 V. Find ID for VDS = 0.3 V and for VDS = 2 V, and state the region in each case.
outline: Overdrive Vov = 1.0 V and region test VDS versus Vov
Linear-region current with the (Vov − VDS/2) factor
Saturation current ½μnCox(W/L)Vov²
Numerical answers with microampere units
Comment that the second value is almost independent of VDS

bank.q: An nMOS with VTH0 = 0.4 V, γ = 0.4 V^0.5 and φF = 0.35 V has its source 0.6 V above the body. Compute the new threshold voltage and the loss in overdrive current for VGS = 1.2 V.
outline: Body-effect formula with VSB substituted
New overdrive compared with the old one
Ratio of saturation currents from the square law
Why stacked transistors in a NAND gate suffer this effect

bank.q: A gate with W = 1 µm, L = 0.1 µm, Cox = 15 fF/µm² and overlap capacitance 0.2 fF/µm per side drives an inverter. Estimate the load capacitance and the delay if the driver resistance is 5 kΩ.
outline: Cox·W·L computation with units
Overlap and junction contributions added
RC delay estimate τ = Req·C
Note that delay scales with W/L ratio and load
Mention that the estimate is a first-order RC model

bank.q: A process is scaled by a constant-field factor S = 2. Work out how VTH, ID, gate capacitance, gate delay and power per gate change.
outline: All dimensions and VDD divided by S
Field stays constant, so VTH scales by 1/S as well
Current scales roughly by 1/S
Capacitance scales by 1/S
Delay scales by 1/S and power per gate by 1/S²
Density rises by S²

bank.q: A transistor has Ioff = 10 nA/µm at 25 °C and a subthreshold swing of 80 mV/decade at room temperature. Estimate the leakage at VGS = 0.2 V below threshold and the effect of a 20 °C rise.
outline: Exponential relation ID ∝ 10^(−VGS/S)
One decade of current per 80 mV
Temperature raises S by roughly 2 to 3 mV/decade per °C
Resulting leakage multiplier
Why leakage sets the standby budget of a phone chip

bank.q: Explain how velocity saturation and channel length modulation each change the square-law model, and say which correction dominates in a 50 nm device.
outline: Assumptions behind the square law: long channel, constant mobility, low field
Mobility degradation with vertical field and the (1 + θVov) denominator
Velocity saturation giving ID ≈ W·vsat·Cox·Vov and the alpha-power form
Channel length modulation factor (1 + λVDS) and its output resistance
Relative importance at short channel length and high overdrive
Effect on gain of an amplifier and on output resistance

bank.q: A measured short-channel nMOS shows current lower than the square law at high VGS and a rising slope in saturation. Explain the causes mathematically and discuss the reliability problems hot carriers, LDD structures and NBTI create.
outline: Reduced current from mobility degradation and velocity saturation
Rising saturation slope from channel length modulation and DIBL
Hot-carrier injection, damage near the drain and why LDD is used
NBTI shifting threshold voltage over the life of a pMOS
Impact on timing margins and on the inverter transfer characteristic

bank.q: Compare a planar bulk nMOS with a FinFET of the same footprint for channel control, leakage, drive current, capacitance and variability.
outline: Gate control on one side versus two or three sides of the channel
Effective width of a fin and the quantised fin count
Lower subthreshold swing and lower off-current
Higher capacitance and layout complexity
Fully depleted channel, lighter body doping, less random dopant fluctuation
Why FinFETs arrived when planar gates lost control below about a quarter micrometre

bank.q: Explain why subthreshold conduction replaced dynamic power as the main worry in scaled CMOS, and evaluate the design knobs available to reduce it.
outline: Exponential subthreshold current and its dependence on VTH and swing
Swing floor of about 60 mV/decade at room temperature
Gate-oxide tunnel current and reverse-biased junction leakage
Knobs: higher VTH, power gating, body bias, multi-threshold libraries, cooler operation
Trade-off between leakage and speed
Why leakage now sets standby battery life

bank.q: Explain the origins of DIBL, GIDL and gate tunnel current in a deep-submicrometre transistor, and discuss how each shows up in measured device data.
outline: Scaling of the drain field into the source end of a short channel
DIBL: threshold shifts downward as VDS rises, off-current rises
GIDL at high VDS and negative or low VGS: band-to-band tunnelling at the drain overlap
Gate tunnel current as tox falls: direct tunnelling through a thin oxide
Signatures in the ID-VGS family of curves and in the off-state leakage plot
Design responses: halo doping, high-k dielectric, thicker equivalent oxide

glossary.def: The surface condition where the gate attracts majority carriers, making the surface richer in the bulk carrier type than the bulk itself.
The layer under the gate that holds no free carriers, only fixed ionised dopant atoms, when the gate pushes majority carriers away.
A thin surface layer of minority carriers, created by a strong gate voltage, that connects source and drain and carries the transistor current.
The gate voltage at which the semiconductor bands are flat, equal to the work-function difference minus the oxide charge effect.
The gate-to-source voltage at which strong inversion starts and a conducting channel just forms.
The increase in threshold voltage caused by a reverse bias between source and body, which adds depletion charge under the gate.
The gate voltage above threshold, VGS − VTH, that determines how much inversion charge the channel holds.
The drain-end condition where VDS equals the overdrive and the inversion charge density becomes zero.
Another name for the saturation region, where the channel is pinched off near the drain and the current is almost flat.
The same as the linear region: the channel is continuous and the transistor acts as a resistor set by the gate voltage.
The small-signal change in drain current for a change in gate voltage, gm = ∂ID/∂VGS, set by μnCox(W/L)Vov in saturation.
The small-signal resistance looking into the drain, r0 = 1/(λID), created by channel length modulation.
The shortening of the effective channel as VDS grows, which raises the saturation current slightly instead of leaving it flat.
The limiting drift velocity of carriers at high lateral field, which makes drain current grow only linearly with overdrive.
The fall of carrier mobility with the vertical gate field, caused by increased surface scattering.
The exponential drain current that flows even when VGS is below threshold, because carriers still surmount the source barrier.
The change in gate voltage needed to change subthreshold current by one decade, quoted in millivolts per decade.
Drain-induced barrier lowering: the fall of threshold voltage with rising drain voltage in a short-channel device.
Gate-induced drain leakage: band-to-band tunnelling current in the drain overlap region when the gate is low and the drain is high.
A carrier that gains high energy from the lateral field and can be injected into the oxide, damaging the device over time.
Lightly doped drain: a lightly doped extension between channel and drain that spreads the field and reduces hot-carrier damage.
A transistor built on a thin silicon fin with a gate wrapped around two or three of its sides, giving better electrostatic control.
The ratio W/L of channel width to channel length, which multiplies the current a transistor can carry.
Cox = εox/tox, the capacitance per unit area of the gate oxide that couples the gate to the channel.
The voltage applied between body and source, used to raise or lower threshold voltage through the body effect.
